blocks.text: In astronomy, measuring the distances to stars and galaxies is essential for understanding the structure and expansion of the universe.

blocks.title: Standard candles
blocks.text: Standard candles are astronomical objects with known intrinsic brightness (luminosity) that serve as tools for measuring cosmic distances.

By comparing how bright a standard candle appears from Earth (its apparent brightness) with how bright it actually is, astronomers can calculate its distance using the inverse-square law of light: from F = L/(4 pi d^2), d = square root of [L / (4 pi F)]. Examples of standard candles are Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae, both of which have predictable luminosities that make them reliable distance indicators (Fig 21.2).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The idea of standard candles dates back to the 1910s, when Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered that Cepheid variable stars pulse in a predictable way. Her work laid the foundation for measuring cosmic distances and the scale of the universe.

A Cepheid star of luminosity 1.0 x 10^30 W gives a measured flux of 1.0 x 10^-12 W m^-2 at the Earth. Find its distance. Solution: d = square root of [L / (4 pi F)] = square root of [1.0 x 10^30 / (4 x 3.14 x 1.0 x 10^-12)] = square root of (8.0 x 10^40) = 2.8 x 10^20 m (about 30 000 light-years).

blocks.prompt: Two stars appear equally bright. One is a standard candle whose true brightness is well known; the other is not. If the standard candle is farther away, what can you say about the true brightness of the second star?
blocks.explanation: The second star is nearer but looks equally bright, so it must be less luminous than the standard candle (by the square of the ratio of their distances).

items: Standard candles: known luminosity (Cepheids, Type Ia supernovae).
Measured flux and F = L/(4 pi d^2) give the distance.
